teach.title: Where somebody is going

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says where somebody is going?

teach.say: When somebody moves towards a place, Latin puts *ad* (to) or *in* (into) in front of that place and gives it **the accusative (the 'to/into' form after ad, in)**: *ad vīllam* — to the house. It answers *quō?*, where to? — a different question from *ubi?*, where.

check.ask: Which word says where the slaves are going?

teach.title: Words in -a take -am
teach.say: A place whose plain form ends in -a ends in -am when you are going to it: *vīlla* → *ad vīllam*, *porta* → *ad portam*, *fenestra* → *ad fenestram*. It is the same -am the object of a verb takes; here the *ad* tells you it is a destination.

check.ask: Ancilla ad ___ it et rosās videt. (fenestra)

teach.title: Words in -us and -um take -um
teach.say: *Hortus* → *in hortum*; *ōstium* → *ad ōstium*. A word already ending in -um does not change at all, which is why *ad ōstium* looks like the plain form: for these words the going-to form and the naming form are the same.

teach.title: *in* with two cases: staying or going
teach.say: *In* takes either case, and the ending is the meaning. *In vīllā*, with -ā, is where he already is. *In hortum*, with -um, is where he is heading. The verb tells you which to expect: *est*, *habitat*, *dormit* stay put, so the noun takes -ā or -ō; *it*, *venit*, *intrat* move, so the noun takes -am or -um.

check.ask: Which of *ātriō* and *cubiculum* is the place she is going to?

teach.title: More than one place: -ās and -ōs
teach.say: Several destinations take -ās from the -a words and -ōs from the -us words: *ad vīllās*, *ad amīcōs*. The adjective with them takes the same ending: *ad vīllās Rōmānās*.

show.say: ad vīllās — the plural ending is -ās

check.ask: Servī fessī ad ___ Rōmānās veniunt. (vīlla, more than one)

teach.title: Towns need no preposition
teach.say: The name of a town goes into the same form but drops *ad* altogether: *Rōmam it* — he goes to Rome; *Tūsculum eunt* — they go to Tusculum. A bare -am or -um on a town name is by itself the whole 'to'.

check.ask: Which word says where the slaves are going?

core.text: Movement towards a place takes *ad* (to), *in* (into) or *sub* (under, going under) with **the accusative (the 'to/into' form after ad, in)**, *accūsātīvus dīrēctiōnis*: *ad vīllam it* = he goes to the villa; *in hortum currit* = he runs into the garden. The question word is *quō?* (where to?). Names of towns and *domum* (home) drop the preposition: *Rōmam it* = he goes to Rome.
*To*, *into*, *towards* mark the goal of a movement: *she went to Rome*. English uses the same *in* for being in and going in; Latin keeps the word but changes the noun's ending.
Going somewhere: *ad*, *in*, *sub* + accusative (-am, -um; plural -ās, -ōs). Town names and *domum* stand alone in the accusative.

invented.la: Māter cum fīliā ad tabernam ambulat.
invented.en: The mother walks to the shop with her daughter.

core.text: *In vīllā* (ablative): in the villa, at rest. *In vīllam* (accusative): into the villa, arriving. The verb usually gives it away: *est*, *habitat*, *dormit* go with the ablative; *it*, *venit*, *currit*, *intrat* with the accusative. The same test works for *sub*.

more.text: From the learner's notes: a destination may be physical, logical or in time; with most prepositions (*contrā*, *per*, *ante*) the accusative is simply the case prepositions take, so 'destination' and 'object of a preposition' need not be told apart. It matters only for *in* and *sub*, which switch to the ablative when nothing moves, and for the bare accusative of towns and *domum* (*vir domum venit* — the man comes home).

Ørberg cap. VI lines up the three questions: *quō?* Rōmam, Tusculum (accusative); *unde?* Rōmā, Tusculō (ablative); *ubi?* Rōmae, Tusculī (locative). *Per* + accusative = through (*per ōstium*, *per portam*), and *ante* / *post* + accusative give a fixed position (*ante tabernam cōnsistunt* — they stop in front of the shop, r08:44.1). A&G §426–427.
